articles.author: Andy Bull
articles.content: Rassie Erasmus has forged an iron bond in his squad but France could push them to breaking point at Twickenham At its best, Test rugby is a game played right out on the edge, where the players push the very limits of what anyone ought to be capable of. Out there the sport sells itself. In those moments it doesn’t matter if you know what a 50-22 is, or whether that was a hip-drop tackle or not, and no one needs a new Hemisphere Shield, or another message on the big screen telling everyone in the stadium to “Make Some Noise!” When it reaches that pitch of incomparable intensity, emotion and endeavour, Test rugby demands your attention whether you know it all or nothing at all. Stretches of this Nations Championship have been played out there, on the farthest reaches of the sport. Wales lived there for 80 minutes in their 35-28 win over the All Blacks a fortnight ago and were rewarded with one of the most famous results in their history. England came closer to it than they had been in a very long time during their own record 37-12 victory against New Zealand a week later. France got there when they were clinging on to their two-point win against South Africa in Paris, so did Ireland in the closing moments in Dublin days later, when they beat the Springboks by three and all the talk of a backlash be damned. Continue reading...

articles.author: Charlotte Higgins
articles.content: When I was reporting on the arts in the 2000s, the view was ‘politics be damned’. But in times of war and catastrophe, cinema becomes committed – as it should In 2004, I was weeks into my new job as the Guardian’s arts correspondent when I was sent off to cover the Cannes film festival for the first time. The opening movie was Wolfgang Petersen’s Troy . Desperate for a news line, I stuck up my hand in the packed press conference, and – nerdy ex-classics student that I was – asked Brad Pitt if there were any analogies to be drawn between the continuing Iraq war and the mythical Trojan war. It was not a crazy question. Art uses myth to reflect on contemporary horrors all the time. The parallels between Homer and the war in the Middle East seemed obvious. A western alliance invaded an eastern nation on a shaky pretext. The killing of thousands had followed – and, at times, a shameful abuse of the defeated. Pitt duly answered gracefully. Continue reading...

articles.author: Andy Hunter
articles.content: Liverpool head coach sees parallels with Athletic v Sociedad derby as he comes up against his old foe David Moyes “I haven’t lived this derby,” Andoni Iraola acknowledged, and yet he already feels it. A former Athletic Bilbao captain coming up against an ex-Real Sociedad head coach needs no instruction on the importance of winning a derby, whether in the Basque country or on Merseyside. But this week, as the Liverpool head coach approaches his first experience of the latter, there has been no escape. “It has been very easy for me here,” says Iraola of his five months on Merseyside. “Family-wise we have settled in really well. People here are very friendly, they love to talk to you but in a very respectful way. This week there has been a lot [of interaction with Liverpool fans], especially with playing big games against United and Everton. ‘We need to win, we need to win,’ they say.” Continue reading...

articles.content: Explaining the England all-rounder and now great-grandfather reveals a career that refuses to fit in a single box Across the Guardian sportsdesk this week it emerged that a young American colleague didn’t know who Ian Botham was. And why should she? She is young and American. And so the rest of us Brit-splained in five sentences, rehearsed here – and edited to make us sound better than we actually did. Botham is comfortably among the top five most famous living British sportspeople, certainly among those of a certain age. In 1981 he won (almost) single‑handed (arguably) the greatest Ashes series by bending it to his will. He was on the front pages as well as back in the 1980s, for soft drugs, suspensions and shagging. He is a member of the House of Lords. He is the most English of sports stars, Australians love him, and his grandson James plays rugby union for Wales, which is why we started talking about him. Continue reading...

articles.author: Alexander Hurst
articles.content: As Anthropic cashes in on the stock market, human-made masterpieces need greater defence from endless extraction Grand Theft Auto VI came out on the same day that Anthropic made its stock market debut. I keep thinking about that coincidence. As more than one tech writer has pointed out, the new GTA took 13 years to make, more than $1bn of investment and involved 9,000 sets of human hands, and it will probably be the last blockbuster video game to be fully free of generative AI. On the day of its release, a group chat with my most gaming-minded male friends erupted in discussion about whether or not video games, and GTA VI specifically, rose to the level of art. Exploring a national park? Yes, that’s there . Badly assemble a coffee table from “Krapea” (the game’s fictional furniture company)? Ditto. Eating a hot dog? Why not. All of it gloriously human in origin. Perhaps that in itself is an argument for how GTA VI crosses the blurry line from entertainment to something more. It is a medium by which human beings offer others a (necessarily incomplete) interpretation of what it’s like to be them in the world, or to try to transcend it. Alexander Hurst writes for Guardian Europe from Paris Continue reading...

articles.author: Ben Lerwill
articles.content: Once a hive of maritime activity, the estuary is now a haven for wildlife – but you don’t have to be a birder to appreciate its tousled beauty Cheshire’s Hadlow Road is a fine railway station. A redbrick building with a cream signal box and a spick-and-span platform, it has neat benches, potted flowers, and a cafe that serves a restorative flat white. But the metal billboards fixed to the brickwork – advertising, among other things, Lever’s Cattle Cakes and Hudson’s Super Soap – are evidence of what really makes the station notable: the last train came through in 1962. “Nearly 65 years ago,” confirms the man repainting the signal box. I sip my coffee and stare along the line. Plenty has changed in this corner of the country since Hadlow Road’s heyday. The rural station is now a preserved heritage attraction, but for almost 100 years it was a stop on a branch line of the Birkenhead Railway. From its westbound platform, passengers and cargo would rumble out towards the coastal town of West Kirby. The trackbed, long since greened over, is now the Wirral Way , a tree-lined path for walkers and cyclists that stretches along the remarkable Dee estuary. Continue reading...

articles.author: Rhik Samadder
articles.content: Gugu Mbatha-Raw meets a devastatingly eligible Richard Madden in this red-button drama for the end times – but it looks like he’s heading up a conspiracy that threatens everyone on Earth. We all have our pros and cons It’s been fun, from a mental health perspective, to hear the government advise the country to Be Ready, stockpiling supplies for an unspecified catastrophe that could happen at any time. What can we realistically do about targeted tech outages, power loss and Russian cyber-attacks? On my last big shop, I half-heartedly doubled up the items, while remaining unconvinced 30 Lindt balls and two bags of Chilli Heatwave Doritos are going to help much when the fireball comes. I’m anxious but lazy, so my doomsday prepping mostly amounts to watching TV that fuels my paranoia. Currently, it’s Trinity (Netflix, from Tuesday 1 December): a political thriller which stars Gugu Mbatha-Raw as Katherine Decker, second in command officer aboard nuclear submarine USS Kansas. After an inexplicable incident above a contested gasfield in the Antarctic nearly starts a war, Decker is horrified to discover a military cover-up. “What happens at sea stays at sea,” warns her captain. Which sounds less like navy protocol, and more like a dinghy of strippers has been chartered for a cadet’s birthday. Decker’s not having it. Continue reading...

articles.content: In this week’s newsletter: Former magician Nathan Fielder pulls some stunning tricks in this docu-drama, proving audiences love a world of weirdness Warning: while this article is spoiler-free for You Can See Everything, it contains spoilers for The Curse I don’t think we knew what to do with You Can See Everything. The documentary drama – in which comedian turned millennial auteur Nathan Fielder is granted unlimited access to disgraced Theranos CEO Elizabeth Holmes – premiered just over a month ago in the US, and only a week ago in the UK. And yet we have already entirely devoured it, dissecting it to death. Our appetite for analysis has been so ferocious that there is almost nothing left to say about the text itself: questions such as, “Was Holmes lying?”, “Was she manipulated?” and “Was Fielder compromised as a film-maker?” have already been discussed ad nauseam. And it is this – the strange, greedy way in which we have treated and received the film – that I have found striking (and, to be frank, frustrating). Continue reading...

articles.content: Fans and famous friends put their nosiest questions to the 91-year-old actor It’s mid-afternoon and Judi Dench and I are sitting in the “den” of her country house in Surrey. It’s one of the smallest rooms in her Elizabethan home: timber beams, terracotta-painted walls, her father’s consulting-room desk and chair within touching distance, together with the bronze “Dr Dench” plaque that used to hang on the railings outside their family home in York. Behind Judi’s head hangs an enormous painting of her as M, presented as a gift on her last day of filming on Skyfall . Through the latticed windows is a view on to the garden, which is crowded with trees she plants for lost friends and family – a beloved oak, a tribute to her late husband, actor Michael Williams, towers above the pond. Even though the room is suffused with autumn sunshine, all the lights are on in the house. Judi has always needed light around her – she’s been afraid of the dark since she was small. Continue reading...

articles.author: Ariel Dorfman
articles.content: Having lived through the real life horror it was chilling to see Martin McDonagh’s film so close to its historical site. Would its audience hear the urgent message? It was chilling for me, as a survivor of the 1973 coup that installed a bloody 17-year dictatorship in Chile, to watch Wild Horse Nine at a theatre in Santiago, a viewing haunted by those who had been killed and disappeared during the reign of General Augusto Pinochet. Though Martin McDonagh’s film is set shortly before the military takeover, it disturbingly foretells the atrocities that are to come, a terrifying future that is known to the protagonists, Chris and Lee, because, as CIA agents, they have been instrumental in the conspiracy to destroy the peaceful revolution of democratically elected president Salvador Allende. Continue reading...

articles.content: A Christmas party mix of moreishy savoury, spicy, salty and citrussy bites to suit every palate. It should feel generous, delicious, easy to eat, and simple enough to put together, not least so the host can enjoy the festivities, too. ’Tis the season for crunchy, salty snacks such as my dangerously addictive tom yum party mix that can be scarfed by the fistful, a refreshing citrus salad piled up on the best edible vessel, namely chicory, and sprouts on sticks with peanut sauce that can be passed around. Importantly, all of these leave one hand free for a glass of something deliciously festive. Happy Christmas everyone! Continue reading...

articles.author: Guardian staff and agencies
articles.content: Ukrainian leader likens Putin to Hitler; laser system intercepts Russian drone but not ready for ‘mass deployment’. What we know on day 1,739 Volodymyr Zelenskyy has criticised Donald Trump for calling Vladimir Putin his “friend” , likening the Russian leader to Adolf Hitler . “Of course it’s up to the president of the United States, but ... it’s strange,” the Ukrainian leader told the BBC in an interview aired on Friday. “He is an aggressor, and a killer... He can’t be a friend. Just cannot be. It’s the same that somebody says about Hitler during the second world war, that he’s a good friend. No. He’s not a friend.” Zelenskyy said what was needed was “more progress” and urged Washington to increase pressure on Moscow. Ukraine has for the first time used a laser weapon to shoot down a Russian jet-powered drone , according to its state-backed defence group Brave1. An adviser to Zelenskyy, Serhiy Beskrestnov, published footage earlier this week showing a target crashing in a fireball, saying a Russian Geran jet drone had been shot down by a laser system for the “first time”. Agence France-Presse quoted Brave1 as saying on Friday: “Footage recently emerged online showing a Ukrainian laser system being used in combat to intercept an enemy jet-powered drone.” The weapon was developed by a recipient of a Brave1 grant and operated by a private air defence team, Brave1 added. But it cautioned that “a first successful interception does not mean the technology is ready for mass deployment”. “Laser air defence remains an experimental technology,” it said, adding that at least seven teams in Ukraine were currently working on laser weapons. Beskrestnov said the system, known as Blysk and developed by the Ukrainian company Carmine Sky, was protecting critical infrastructure during the interception. A convoy of Russian ships carrying military vehicles bound for Libya has turned around in the Mediterranean after Ukrainian maritime drones sank ⁠a Russian naval warship in Benghazi ⁠port last Sunday, Reuters quoted ​three people from military and security services as saying on Friday. The convoy, which was escorted by the Russian navy frigate Golovko, turned around near the strait of Sicily on the same day as ⁠the attack in Benghazi, said a European military official who had been tracking the convoy. A Ukrainian military intelligence official and a Middle East security official confirmed the flotilla had turned from heading to Libya. Russia’s defence ministry did not immediately respond to a request for comment. Ukraine has offered ⁠a Black Sea ceasefire to enable food ⁠exports and ⁠passed this ​on to international allies , the foreign minister ⁠said. “We are ready for ⁠a ceasefire. We are ​grateful to ‌India, Turkey and ‌Egypt, which are playing ‌an active and important role in de-escalating tensions in the Black Sea, as well as in mediation efforts. ‌We are now awaiting a response from ​Russia,” Andrii Sybiha was cited by public broadcaster Suspilne as saying on Friday. He added that Russia had proposed ⁠Ukraine suspend attacks on the ​Russian ​oil sector under ​the truce, but ​Kyiv ‌would only consider ​this ​as part of a bigger energy ceasefire deal. Ukraine’s military said on ⁠Friday it ⁠had struck ​a Russian solid ⁠rocket fuel production site ⁠in ​the Tula ‌region south ‌of Moscow ‌overnight. “The plant is the starting point of the ‌missile production chain: it manufactures ​components for plastic explosives and ⁠the polymer used ​to produce ​solid ​propellant for ​Russian ‌ballistic missiles,” ​the ​defence ministry said on Telegram. Russia’s foreign ministry has accused ⁠Latvia of creating artificial ⁠obstacles ⁠to hinder the ​transit of Russian grain to ⁠global markets , saying the restrictions pose additional risks ⁠to global food security. Ministry ​spokesperson ‌Maria Zakharova ‌claimed in a statement published ‌on the ministry’s website on Friday that Latvia was conducting inspections of Russian grain shipments for allegedly ‌stolen Ukrainian agricultural products and was seeking ways ​to ban Russian grain transit altogether. Continue reading...

articles.content: Tomoka Nishiyama will soon compete against men in professional shogi, often known as Japanese chess, but women remain marginalised in the popular game Encouragement was in short supply when, in the 1960s, Akiko Takojima set her sights on becoming an elite shogi player. Women were too “stupid” to excel at the Japanese board game, a male instructor told her, before suggesting she find something else to occupy her time. Decades after Takojima and five others became the first female professionals, a 100-year-old barrier in the game is about to be broken. From April, Tomoka Nishiyama will turn shogi’s gender bias on its head when she becomes the first woman to compete against men at the highest level of the game. Continue reading...

articles.content: Marvel Stadium, Melbourne The energy is infectious at Styles’s first night in Melbourne with a hit-packed set creating a jubilant atmosphere It’s been 16 years since the world met a floppy-haired boy who worked at a bakery on The X Factor. Half his lifetime later, that boy is on a record-breaking residency tour, playing 30 shows at New York City’s Madison Square Garden and 12 at London’s Wembley Stadium. Luckily for Australia, Sydney and Melbourne are two of just seven cities on the itinerary for Harry Styles’ Together, Together tour in 2026. On the first of four nights at Melbourne’s Marvel Stadium, the forecast is gloomy (chances of flash floods and thunderstorms) – but the mood is jubilant (and the roof is closed). Reflecting Styles’s penchant for business casual chic on this tour, ties are the uniform of the evening among fans, bedazzled with glitter and draped over sparkly tops. Mothers and daughters in matching attire stand in front of the stadium, taking selfies. (My favourite fan sign of the night: “My mum heard you like older women.”) The 18-year-old sitting beside me has travelled from regional Victoria for her first concert. A man points to my 2015 One Direction tour T-shirt. “I went to that!” he proclaims, and we exchange smiles. We might all be strangers, but here it’s all love. Continue reading...

articles.content: 3rd v 3rd: Ireland 38-14 Australia Henshaw, Timoney and Baloucoune also scored tries Ireland’s quality told in the end. Back-to-back victories to finish the year would have been a tonic for a much-criticised Wallabies team and while they started strongly, they were ultimately outclassed. They have lost seven matches in a row against Ireland: there was a time when such a statistic would have been unimaginable. Sam Prendergast kicked brilliantly, off the tee and from hand, to orchestrate a success that was a classic Irish blend of power and finesse. The fly-half scored 13 points off the tee and his tactical kicking was world-class too. Two Ireland victories against the Wallabies have come in the Nations Championship and this was more one-sided than the 33-31 thriller in July . Continue reading...

articles.author: Bernie Sanders
articles.content: At this pivotal moment in American history, let us move forward together to take on and defeat a powerful, greedy and corrupt ruling class We are at a pivotal moment in history. Never before in human history have so few people held so much wealth and so much power. And never before have we seen such an unprecedented level of greed, arrogance and irresponsibility on the part of the world’s ruling class. Here is the good news: leaders from around the world are finally starting to wake up. This week, elected officials and economists from around the world – including four Nobel prize winners – came together in Paris for a “Summit Against International Oligarchy”. As the summit’s proclamation stated, “The explosion of extreme wealth is the major social fact of our time … We are sounding the alarm: billionaires are a threat to our democracies.” Bernie Sanders is a US senator, and ranking member of the health, education, labor and pensions committee. He represents the state of Vermont and is the longest-serving independent in the history of Congress Continue reading...

articles.content: A sensational start for the Italian was swiftly followed by a dismal run and long faces in the team This is the great known unknown in Manchester City’s run of one win – in addition to victory on penalties against Brighton in the Carabao Cup – in seven matches. After guilty verdicts were returned regarding the breaking of Premier League financial rules, Enzo Maresca’s team went to Anfield and handed Liverpool a 3-0 schooling . Yet this proved the falsest of dawns, with Andoni Iraola’s nascent side perhaps caught in a bad moment. City have since managed one league victory ( 3-2 over Ipswich , six days later) and two more wins in regulation time (in the Champions League) in 10 matches. The sequence includes one point from the past four league fixtures. Maresca argues that his, too, is an embryonic project so there will be uneven form. “I am not a magician,” he said on Friday. But it is also fair to ponder whether, after the adrenaline surge of an us-against-the-world mentality carried City to the Liverpool and Ipswich wins, the grim reality of what the guilty verdict may mean for careers is affecting players. City have appealed against the ruling, saying they are “innocent of the accusations”. Continue reading...

articles.content: Maro Itoje says the team have used morale-sapping defeats this year to reach this stage but there is ‘more to come’ Offer England’s players a choice between a cut-price “Black Friday” deal and another super soaraway All Black Saturday and this week’s answer is unanimous. This may be an opportune moment to snap up pre-Christmas bargains on the high street but Maro Itoje and his side are rather more intent on securing a priceless little chunk of history. Never before in 121 years have England’s men beaten New Zealand in three consecutive Tests and the last time their opponents lost six times in a calendar year was back in 1949. During that distant annus horribilis the All Blacks ended up contesting simultaneous Test series against South Africa and Australia and lost them both; this time around there would be no such asterisk. Continue reading...

articles.author: Jonathan Freedland
articles.content: To get Jensen Huang back at Nvidia, the president trampled on the justice system, national security and the trust America needs to do business in the global economy Don’t let the sex distract you. Or the lies or the boardroom intrigue or even the AI-generated bra, all of which could have come from an especially wild episode of Succession. Don’t let that lure you into thinking that the Jensen Huang affair is, as Donald Trump would have it, little more than a sex scandal involving a corporate maestro. It is much more serious than that. The events of the past week tell instead a story of legal immunity and indeed impunity – revealing how Trump is putting himself, the tech bros and even artificial intelligence above the law. It can be hard to see that through the thicket of questions that surround this episode, each one of which, don’t get me wrong, merits attention. Consider the personal profit Trump made thanks to his re-installation of Huang as the CEO of Nvidia, the world’s leading maker of advanced AI chips. Breaking the norm observed by previous presidents who, keen to avoid even the appearance of a conflict of interest, either divested themselves of stock holdings or placed them in a blind trust, Trump cheerfully buys and sells stocks in companies whose fates he can influence. He saw the value of his shares in Nvidia plunge when Huang was forced out, following revelations that the CEO had had an affair with Alice Huang, reportedly an asset of Chinese intelligence. Last weekend Trump urged the board to reconsider; Huang was reinstated on Monday and Nvidia’s value promptly soared – putting $15m in Trump’s pocket . Not for the first time, he had used the power of his office to enrich himself. Jonathan Freedland is a Guardian columnist Do you have an opinion on the issues raised in this article? articles.author: Editorial
articles.content: Machines are solving problems that have been beyond the reach of human ingenuity. Their growing power must not become the sole preserve of billionaires For the average person, the news that AI has helped crack a problem that has defied mathematicians since 1859 might elicit momentary awe. What ought to worry everyone is not the discovery per se, but what it says about the power of the machines making it. The pace of scientific discovery looks like it is outrunning the ability of humanity – and its institutions – to understand, let alone regulate, AI’s advances. Last Friday Levent Alpöge , a mathematician at Anthropic, said that he, with the assistance of an unreleased version of the company’s Claude chatbot, had produced what many mathematicians see as the holy grail: a proof for the Riemann hypothesis . Mathematicians like Cornell University’s Steven Strogatz had already cried on podcasts, lamenting that students were asking: “What’s the point if the AI can do math better than any human being?” Computers can validate the Alpöge-Claude proof. But Prof Strogatz fears AI’s discoveries may soon defy human understanding. Asking AI to explain them, he said, would be like him trying to teach calculus to his own dog. articles.author: Editorial
articles.content: In a landscape dominated by the same names and celebrity authors, this new award shines a spotlight on great titles that might have been overlooked “Why shouldn’t a great children’s book have the same status as a great adult book?” asked Frank Cottrell-Boyce, the former children’s laureate and chair of the inaugural Children’s Booker prize , as the shortlist was announced this week. In nearly 60 years of the adult prize, the only children’s book to have made the longlist is Philip Pullman’s The Amber Spyglass in 2001. Now children’s fiction has its own Booker, with four of the seven judges aged between eight and 12. Crucially, the kids get the casting vote. The shortlist, “the great eight”, includes five novels, two graphic novels and an illustrated collection of short stories. Big names such as Eoin Colfer, Liz Hyder and Shaun Tan appear alongside less established writers. There is time travel, humour and sci-fi fantasy, in novels dealing with war, grief and identity. Do you have an opinion on the issues raised in this article? articles.content: FBI estimates thousands of people identify as members, or recent members, of group linked to indecent images of girls and blackmail It sounds benign: the Com, short for the Community. But crime agencies around the world warn that it is far from that and the young cybercriminals involved are causing havoc and putting children at chilling, sickening risk. Beau-Jack Mensforth was jailed by a UK judge on Friday for his activities as part of the Com. He was one individual operating from his bedroom in north-east England, but there are probably thousands more like him and parents are being urged by police to be aware and to check their children’s devices. articles.author: Guardian Staff
articles.content: Colin Montgomery suggests that expectations should be properly managed. Plus letters from Paul Hartley , Hartley Dean and Peter Thornton John Harris’s jeremiad about what the world of work has become ( A truism for our political leaders: until work again involves respect and decent levels of pay, this crisis will continue, 22 November ) put me in mind of the old joke: “How do I get to Dublin?” “Well, I wouldn’t start from here.” Because, as he concludes, there’s almost no chance of any government being able to even begin to relieve this situation quickly, short of putting an emergency brake on 40 years of neoliberalism. As if. I’d like to suggest a real starting point for the fightback against this seemingly interminable malaise that looks set to blight generations to come: namely, begin from somewhere grounded in properly managed expectations. Because arguably, that’s what underpins all of this: we’ve all been cynically inveigled into a bargain that can never be fulfilled. Continue reading...

articles.content: Willemina Rietsema , a GP, says no explanation doesn’t mean no physical illness, it just means we haven’t found one (yet). Carrie Eckersley thinks we need to consider the wider context in which symptoms develop Regarding Huw Green’s article ( How can we explain psychosomatic illnesses?, 22 November ), the body and the mind/brain have strong connections both ways. It is therefore not surprising that major psychological distress can lead to physical symptoms, and the other way around. However, as a GP, I would recommend being extremely careful about equating “otherwise unexplained symptoms” with psychosomatic illness. No explanation doesn’t mean no physical illness, it just means we haven’t found one (yet). Continue reading...

articles.content: Male sexual violence against women is fuelled by misogyny, writes Sarah Mulholland The courage of Joanne Young is powerful, and it could be pivotal ( Joanne Young praised for bravery in exposing rape by husband and strangers, 20 November ). The publicity given to high-profile cases such as those of Russell Brand, Jeffrey Epstein and Mohamed Al Fayed is understandable, but it runs the risk of serving as a convenient deflector, allowing us to comfort ourselves that rapists and sexual abusers are somehow “other”. Indeed, one of the most pernicious rape myths is the belief that rape is perpetrated by men of a different social or economic status, of a different ethnicity or culture – outsiders from whom we can distance ourselves. Continue reading...

articles.content: Costly on-track clashes have caused tensions to simmer and team need recent talks to tell at Sunday’s Qatar Grand Prix There is an unmistakable air of deja vu heading into the Qatar Grand Prix and with it an intense scrutiny that might be considered unusual for a dead-rubber weekend. Yet for Ferrari, who are the subject of the attention after costly on-track incidents between the teammates Lewis Hamilton and Charles Leclerc, more pertinent is how it might play out if the conflicts are not resolved and the Scuderia are in a title fight next season. Hamilton and Leclerc clashed on track at the last round in Las Vegas, only two weeks after similarly contesting a place in Mexico cost them a potential one-two. The team principal Fred Vasseur was furious then, saying it displayed a lack of respect for the team and was unacceptable. They held talks to resolve the issue at the next round in Brazil. Continue reading...

articles.author: Stuart Heritage
articles.content: After a 12-year run, Amelia Dimoldenberg’s last episode of Chicken Shop Date – a therapy session with Esther Perel – is being shown in cinemas. It’s a fittingly grand finale for a YouTube cult favourite that far outgrew its medium The decision to screen the full final series of Chicken Shop Date in cinemas before the finale airs on YouTube is, it could be argued, overkill. The cinema is a place where you sit rapt among like-minded people, bombarded with cutting-edge sound design and world-class visuals. On the other hand, the fun interview show that is Chicken Shop Date is the thing I watch alone on my computer while I pick my toenails. It isn’t a natural fit, is what I’m trying to say. And yet, goddamn it if the whole thing didn’t leave me slightly choked up. After 12 years of flirting and awkwardness, Amelia Dimoldenberg’s final guest is Esther Perel, the Belgian psychotherapist and relationship guru beloved by Oprah Winfrey. It is by no means a traditional episode, almost completely dismissing the tone of everything that came before it. Dimoldenberg’s well-honed persona, alternately dismissive and needy, is nowhere to be seen. Instead, Dimoldenberg does something that Perel must be deadeningly familiar with when meeting new people: she uses the episode as a free therapy session. Continue reading...

articles.content: Trump’s son-in-law and senior negotiator paints Russian invasion of Ukraine as a misunderstanding to be resolved In the space of a 70-minute interview, Jared Kushner – Donald Trump’s son-in-law and a prominent US negotiator in Russia, Gaza and Iran – probably did more to reveal why the world is mired in entrenched conflicts than a thousand geopolitical tomes or seminars. During the conversation this week with Mathias Döpfner, the chief executive of the Axel Springer media publisher, Kushner gave a rare insight into his diplomatic technique, offering a string of homilies that veered close to banalities: “You have nothing until you have something”, “diplomacy is like untying knots on a fishing line for his son”, and “you play the ball from where it lands”. Continue reading...

articles.content: Sign up now! Sign up now! Sign up now? Sign up now! A few weeks ago, Alessio Dionisi was forced to deny the “fake news” he had joined Sean Dyche, Gianfranco Zola, Beppe Sannino, Óscar García, Billy McKinlay, Slavisa Jokanovic, Quique Sánchez Flores (twice), Walter Mazzarri, Marco Silva, Javi Gracia (twice), Nigel Pearson, Vladimir Ivic, Xisco Muñoz, Claudio Ranieri, Roy Hodgson, Rob Edwards, Slaven Bilic, Chris Wilder, Valérien Ismael, Tom Cleverley, Paulo Pezzolano and Edward Still in being sacked by the Pozzo family since 2012. There was no denial on Sunday, when the axe inevitably fell on the head coach following a 4-0 shellacking at Sheffield United and the Italian left after only 18 games in charge. While his reign is unlikely to live long in the memory of anyone at Vicarage Road, Dionisi can at least boast on his LinkedIn page that in terms of longevity under the Pozzos, he took charge of 18 more matches than Dyche, 17 more than García and 16 more than McKinlay. Indeed, he even outlasted Rob Edwards, who was assured he would be backed “come hell or high water” upon his 2022 appointment, only to be fired from the ejector seat 11 games later. Continue reading...

articles.content: The Vaults, London X Factor’s Diana Vickers leads this trip back to the 00s, as JM Barrie’s story is retooled as a night of pop bangers How about if Peter Pan, refusing to grow up, was a stunted man-boy lost in the what-ifs of his youth? He might be the promoter of a noughties club night, stuck in his glory days where everyone’s dressed like Girls Aloud meets the Vengaboys and the world hasn’t yet gone into meltdown. NVRLAND is that club, and this show – created by Steven Kunis and Jack Holden – is halfway between a jukebox musical and a cheesy disco, masterminded, surely, for the Christmas party crowd to down oversweet cocktails before oversharing with someone they barely know from the finance department. It’s basically pantomime for millennials/zillennials, with lots of audience participation from the dancefloor. And after a bit of warming up, it is great, giddy fun. Continue reading...

articles.content: Club activate option and plan further talks with captain ‘I am not nice,’ says Pochettino as he targets improvement Manchester United have triggered a clause to extend the captain Bruno Fernandes’ contract until the summer of 2028 on a day when Mauricio Pochettino warned his players they should not expect him to be “nice” in his attempts to turn around the club’s fortunes. articles.author: Robert Hutton
articles.content: He’s perennially disgraced and yet he just won’t go away – now he’s joined the latest Brexit debate. Isn’t there a mute button, or an exile plan that really works? What a week it has been for Indispensable Men. In the old days, if someone were forced to resign, whether as ambassador to Washington or boss of a trillion-dollar company, they would become what we quaintly used to call “disgraced”. Perhaps they would spend the rest of their days volunteering with a charity. Certainly, for a good decade afterwards, they would acquire the journalistic epithet “shamed” on first mention. Later – much later – they might be allowed back into public life, in some lesser role where they could be discreetly supervised, to check exactly how many emails they were sending to which people arranging what holidays. But what’s this we find over on news website UnHerd? Why, it’s a 2,000-word essay from one Peter Mandelson on the difficulties of rejoining the European Union. Mandelson … Mandelson. That name definitely rings a bell. Let’s see if there’s a clue at the bottom of the piece. Ah, yes: “Peter Mandelson is a former cabinet minister and EU Trade Commissioner.” That’s the chap: Gordon Brown’s former business secretary. Though I feel as if I’ve seen his name in the news a bit more recently than 2010. Might he be a “former” anything else? Continue reading...

articles.author: Tom Perkins
articles.content: Experts say NIH research raises concerns about chemical companies’ influence on US agency’s pesticide division The US government’s top medical research agency has released three new studies linking glyphosate, the world’s most widely used pesticide and an active ingredient in Roundup, to cancer . The National Institutes of Health (NIH) findings contradict a controversial recent Environmental Protection Agency (EPA) conclusion that the weedkiller is not a carcinogen, and deals a blow to the White House, which has been closely allied with Roundup’s producer, Bayer. The NIH’s three papers could have significant political and legal fallout. The EPA is in the process of a court-ordered re-evaluation of glyphosate’s cancer risks. The NIH findings generate new pressure for the EPA to find that the substance is linked to cancer, which would subject it to a modest increase in regulations. Continue reading...

articles.author: Rafqa Touma
articles.content: We’ve been brought up on literature about underdogs who fight – and triumph – against an unjust status quo I first read The Hunger Games trilogy in early high school. Set in the post-apocalyptic nation of Panem, society is ruled by the Capitol – they are fascistic, surveil everything, and keep the middle and upper classes quiet with annual reality war games in which lower-class teenagers must fight to the death. Ten years later, in 2020, I was about to enter a newsroom for the first time, at the tail end of Donald Trump’s first presidency. That same year, Suzanne Collins returned to her dystopian world with a prequel. The Ballad of Songbirds and Snakes is set decades before the original trilogy, revealing the origin story of both the games and their architect, President Snow, through his young, possessive perspective. Continue reading...

articles.author: Dominik Diamond
articles.content: While everyone else is giddy over Zelda and GTA, Dominik Diamond finds himself behind the times on a Nintendo Wii I find myself on the wrong side of gaming history this month. I have zero zeitgeist. My takes are as fresh as something found at the rear of the fridge. I haven’t even played Grand Theft Auto VI yet, but we’ll get to that. Worse, all month, the Nintendo sector of the gaming world has been going googly eyed over Zelda. The Ocarina of Time remake seems to have produced more joy than all the puppies in the world. But not for me. I have never liked Zelda. It’s like being a movie reviewer who doesn’t like Disney, or a vegan shark. Continue reading...

articles.author: Natalie Parletta
articles.content: Tens of thousands of people experience strikes each year. What are the effects of a current five times hotter than the sun – and how can you keep safe? Caitlin Thomas recalls knowing that something terrible had happened but not fully understanding what. She and her partner had arrived at a music festival some 270km north of Melbourne in the early afternoon and began setting up their tents and a gazebo for shade when the sky suddenly turned dark and the rain became incredibly heavy. A huge gust of wind picked up and Thomas asked her partner to hold on to the gazebo so it wouldn’t fly away. “He then asked me to hold on to it also so he could crack open his beer.” Continue reading...

articles.content: Environmental and animal welfare concerns, and taste preferences, are behind rising popularity of vegan alternatives Has milk gotta lotta bottle? It may not have as much as it used to, with official data showing Britons are buying less cow’s milk than at any point since records began. Guardian analysis of the government’s family food survey shows the average person bought 1.8 pints (1,024ml) of cow’s milk a week in 2024-25 – the lowest level in the record’s 52-year history and less than half the amount of milk bought in 1974. Continue reading...

Data published on Friday showed at least 3,276 people sleeping rough were offered a route off the street in October, under the new scheme announced by the prime minister on his first day in office . That compares with an estimated 9,369 who slept rough across England in September, the latest month where data was available. Continue reading...

articles.author: Ben Child
articles.content: Working out where returning hero Steve Rogers has been is only one of the multiversal puzzles fans must now get their heads around – which is catnip for the connoisseurs The cinema release of Avengers: Doomsday is now roughly three weeks away and, judging by the final trailer , we’re living in the one timeline where every loose end Marvel has left dangling for years is now worth tugging on. Even the ones we thought the studio had tied up rather nicely. Ever since it became apparent that Chris Evans’ Steve Rogers would be returning in the new film, along with next year’s sequel Avengers: Secret Wars, fans have been asking themselves: where exactly has he been all this time? Now, thanks to the latest footage, we’re beginning to get an idea, and we might also be starting to pick up clues as to why Doctor Doom would take an interest in his new postcode. One of the most startling aspects of the new trailer is the arrival of the Fantastic Four, led by Pedro Pascal’s Reed Richards, on Rogers’ front lawn. We’ve known since the finale of Avengers: Endgame that Steve used Tony Stark’s newly discovered time-travelling tech to go back to the 1940s and live out his life with Peggy Carter during the events of that film – but until recently it seemed most likely that happened in good old Earth-616, the main Marvel Cinematic Universe continuity. Continue reading...

articles.author: Laura Snapes
articles.content: Co-op Live, Manchester Bridgers caused some controversy by banning phones on her Lost Weekend tour, but the intimacy and attention it forces feels as much a gift to fans as it does to her The giant white dome that hangs over Phoebe Bridgers’ stage looks like Disney World’s Epcot, Walt’s “experimental prototype community of tomorrow” envisioning how we might live better. Bridgers’ tour is its own utopia: everyone’s phones are locked away, an edict that caused some controversy among younger fans who have never experienced a gig any other way. Down our aisle, none of us know the time and two teenage fans wearing skeleton outfits (Bridgers’ old stagewear staple) faux-complain that they’ve actually had to talk to each other. It’s so unusual not to see a speckle of screens at an arena show that, from the seats looking down on the standing area, it feels as if there’s been some kind of power cut, or we’re in a protected natural dark reserve. The decision seemed made to protect the sanctity of the pain in Bridgers’ third album. Lost Weekend swims in her conflicted feelings over her sometimes-estranged father’s death, given his abuse of her mother, and the end of Bridgers’ fairytale engagement, after she realised she wanted something different. Continue reading...

articles.author: Zoe Williams
articles.content: The MasterChef judge on artichokes, ambition and Irish food It’s an amazing moment when Anna Haugh lets me peel and chop a butternut squash, right there in the kitchen next to her, while she makes a beetroot pickle. The 46-year-old is a fiendish perfectionist and a fierce champion of every last ingredient. She’s making a dish that reflects the sensibility of her restaurant, Myrtle , named after the giant, dynastic wellspring of the Irish food scene, Myrtle Allen . It’s polenta with squash two ways – crushed and pureed – with pickle and goat’s cheese. Every ingredient has a story, and every story reaches back into an epic food tradition. There’s a lot going on, though you really have to see it to know just how much; so although I have the potential to really mess things up, here she has no choice but to let me peel and chop. Elite cooking while talking like a Bren gun is a skill she’s honed, first in cookery demos “talking to a plastic bag and a stray dog, and you’d be lucky if someone came over to shelter from the rain”; then on Saturday Kitchen – a trial by fire: “Everything is easy after that. I could do any cookery programme now. I even tried to persuade them to do the MasterChef final live.” Continue reading...

articles.content: No ground in Australia is more associated with ritual guttings of English cricket teams than the so-called Gabbatoir. They usually leave in a state of disarray, beaten up on the field and with ears still ringing from abuse on the boundary’s edge. Yet on a muggy Friday night on Vulture Street, the locals had precious little material to work with and the traditional script was flipped on its head. Driven by Jamie Overton’s fiery five-wicket haul, England wiped the floor with their hosts for the second match in a row to claim a 2-1 lead with two to play. Continue reading...

articles.author: Oliver Wainwright
articles.content: Repurposing a space previously used for selling Citroëns, the Belgian capital now has its first ever dedicated space for contemporary art. It’s certainly ambitious – but will they be able to fill it? ‘A cathedral of cars” is how the colossal Citroën garage in Brussels was described when it opened in 1934, conceived as a startling glass temple to showcase the streamlined wonders of the automobile age. It greeted the street with an immense curtain wall of glass that wrapped a monumental nave-like showroom, culminating in a curved art deco prow, which glowed like a crystal lantern by night. Almost a century later, arts and culture have replaced cars as the great urban consumables of our age. Consequently, after a €230m decade-long transformation in collaboration with the Pompidou Centre, this gargantuan garage has been reborn as a palace of performance, dance, music, film, architecture and visual art. The original Parisian Pompidou was designed as a transformable cultural machine for the city ; this place takes those urban ambitions to an even greater extreme. Continue reading...

articles.author: Daniel Dylan Wray
articles.content: She started out scribbling 19th-century workers’ songs on receipts at her retail job. Now, the folk disruptor is taking them global – and finding resonances with today’s injustices When Jennifer Reid was working in Home Bargains, she used till receipts to write out the folk ballads she was learning by heart, and then tucked them into her waistband, because staff uniforms didn’t have pockets. “Or if it was too sweaty in summer, I’d hide them behind the shampoo bottles and then go back for them,” she recalls. Growing up in Middleton, Greater Manchester, Reid discovered local broadside ballads – single-sheet songs sold on the street depicting life and events, which boomed during the Industrial Revolution – when volunteering at Chetham’s Library in her late teens. Reid describes her years prior to this as being “a cantankerous young ’un with all this energy that was sometimes misdirected into antisocial stuff” but this new direction was mind-expanding. “I’d never thought about Oldham or Rochdale in a historical cultural context before,” she says. “Very soon I realised: I want to make sure this history doesn’t die.” Continue reading...

articles.author: Claire Ratinon
articles.content: These exotics can bear plenty of fruit, but you will need a firm hand to stop them dominating your patch You might imagine figs would be tricky to grow in cooler climates like the UK’s (heatwaves aside). But you’d be wrong! Figs can do remarkably well – some might say too well – in this segment of the northern hemisphere. In favourable conditions, fig trees can be quite the thug, inclined to take up any and all the space available for their roving roots. One enormous specimen behind a train station near where I grew up has been there for decades, occupying an impressive number of square metres. You can, of course, purchase a fig tree from a plant nursery. But the two I have in my garden were both grown from hardwood cuttings taken when the parent plant was dormant, which makes now a good time to give this slow but generally reliable process a try. Alternatively, you can wait until spring and seek out a parent plant that’s producing suckers to pot up. Continue reading...

articles.content: Heavy rain, strong winds and coastal flooding creating hazardous conditions for millions travelling for holiday King tides and huge waves have been battering both coasts of the US during a turbulent Thanksgiving period, with severe weather threatening millions across the country. Along the California coast, king tides caused considerable damage. In Pacifica, south of San Francisco, large waves battered the coastline on Wednesday, destroying part of a pier and sending debris into the ocean. The National Weather Service issued coastal flood warnings covering parts of the Pacific coastline and shorelines around San Francisco Bay and San Pablo Bay. Several beachfront properties in Pacifica have already experienced flooding, while authorities in Marin County temporarily issued an evacuation warning for residents of beachfront homes at Stinson Beach. Continue reading...

articles.author: George Francis Lee
articles.content: From Helsinki to Istanbul, independent developers are putting Grand Theft Auto-style action on their home streets, and without billion-dollar budgets. They tell us how they do it Like most kids who shouldn’t have been playing Grand Theft Auto III in 2001, Eamonn Swayah imagined a version of Rockstar Games’ groundbreaking criminal sandbox set in his own back yard. In his case, that was a Manchester council estate, complete with local accents, driving on the left, and plenty of ways to hustle. He didn’t know it, but swapping the game’s facsimile of early 2000s New York City for a different setting was an idea he shared with many watchful game developers. Rockstar’s 3D open world template, it turned out, could be plonked in just about any location, so long as it had people and enough cars to run them over with. After GTA III attracted immense commercial success (and controversy), dozens of copycats and spiritual sequels hit the market throughout the 00s and 2010s. Gamers had a pithy name for them: “GTA clones”. Continue reading...

articles.author: Stuart Heritage
articles.content: Fast becoming an essential Christmas tradition, the Sherlock creator’s latest in this classic horror series – starring Martin Freeman, effectively playing Charles Dickens – is inventive, joyous and, at times, genuinely terrifying For all the doom and gloom about the death of Christmas television as a collective event – nice try bunging on a normal Friday schedule with the word “Christmas” in front of each show, ITV, but we see you – can we at least agree that the most unsung festive TV tradition is Mark Gatiss’s continued revival of A Ghost Story for Christmas? For years now, it has functioned as a dark mirror to the Julia Donaldson animations. Each new episode is small and self-contained, clearly made on a shoestring but containing at least one moment of bone-deep foundational horror. And, as much as this might make the purists clutch their pearls, I would argue that the Gatiss run – starting in earnest in 2018 after a 2013 one-off, with a fallow year for Covid – deserves to be seen as the pinnacle of the series. True, the 1970s version contained classics including The Signalman and A Warning to the Curious, but only eight of those were made. The Bride’s Chamber is Gatiss’s ninth. Continue reading...

articles.author: Sarah Wynn-Williams
articles.content: Since writing her bestselling exposé, the former employee has been forbidden from speaking publicly about Meta. In an exclusive extract from her Orwell lecture, she talks about corporate lawfare, and the growing backlash against NDAs George Orwell understood that what is missing often tells you more than what is there. In Nineteen Eighty-Four, there is a slot in the wall covered by a wire grate. They call it the memory hole. When a document becomes inconvenient to the authorities – a photograph that contradicts the official line, a newspaper that remembers the wrong promise, a name that is no longer supposed to exist – you simply feed it into the slot, whereupon it is whirled away on a current of warm air to enormous hidden furnaces where it burns. The Party doesn’t argue with the past. It removes it. Controlling the past is one of its central tools of power: “Who controls the past controls the future: who controls the present controls the past.” Continue reading...

articles.author: Louis Staples
articles.content: The so-bad-it’s-good holiday film has become a new festive tradition. Stars Maddie Ziegler and Dennis Quaid explain why they’re so hard to resist “With the state of the world right now, people want an escape,” says Maddie Ziegler. The 24-year-old performer first shot to fame on the Lifetime reality show Dance Moms in 2011, before becoming the unlikely muse of the publicity-shy singer Sia , which led to a role in Steven Spielberg ’s West Side Story. Ziegler’s latest project is In a Holidaze , a fuzzy Christmas movie that comes to Netflix on 2 December. “I’ve actually never done a romcom before,” she says, speaking on a recent Zoom call from Los Angeles. “I grew up loving Christmas movies so much, so when this came into my lap, I was so excited.’” In the film, Ziegler plays Maelyn – a restless twentysomething who finds herself trapped in a holiday time-loop, where she’s forced to relive the same Christmas at her family’s picturesque cabin until she learns to trust her gut and take chances on what makes her happy. This sugary-sweet movie might be new territory for Ziegler, but it’s exactly the type of film we’ve come to expect from Netflix. The streamer’s Christmas originals usually revolve around romance and family, with an aesthetic quality and winking irony that feels similar to Hallmark – the American card-maker turned movie giant, whose very name is synonymous with cliches. Continue reading...

articles.author: Flora Willson
articles.content: Queen Elizabeth Hall, London George Benjamin and Martin Crimp’s opera was given a skeletal staging where every detail spoke volumes, leaving the LPO to shine in the spotlight It is always a shock to realise how little apparatus theatre really needs. Dan Ayling’s semi-staging of George Benjamin and Martin Crimp ’s 2018 opera played out across a shallow strip in front of the London Philharmonic Orchestra, with singers occasionally slipping between conductor Edward Gardner and the front desks of the strings. Props were minimal but significant: a skipping rope, a glass tumbler, a pot containing a child’s ashes, a crown spotlit on a velvet cushion. There was no set, just five chairs on one side of the podium and one on the other: a succinct image of isolation, of power dynamics skewed. The protagonists of this grim drama about Edward II – the King, his lover, Gaveston, his wife, Isabel, her ally Mortimer – wore sleek black tie except utilitarian, ambitious, underdressed Mortimer. As the Boy was manoeuvred into position as Young King, tenor James Way not only stood taller and held himself more pugnaciously but also put on a tie: every detail spoke volumes. Continue reading...

Dan Ayling’s semi-staging of George Benjamin and Martin Crimp ’s 2018 opera played out across a shallow strip in front of the London Philharmonic Orchestra, with singers occasionally slipping between conductor Edward Gardner and the front desks of the strings. Props were minimal but significant: a skipping rope, a glass tumbler, a pot containing a child’s ashes, a crown spotlit on a velvet cushion. There was no set, just five chairs on one side of the podium and one on the other: a succinct image of isolation, of power dynamics skewed. The protagonists of this grim drama about Edward II – the King, his lover, Gaveston, his wife, Isabel, her ally Mortimer – wore sleek black tie except utilitarian, ambitious, underdressed Mortimer. As the Boy was manoeuvred into position as Young King, tenor James Way not only stood taller and held himself more pugnaciously but also put on a tie: every detail spoke volumes. Continue reading...

articles.content: (Phantasy Sound) One of the buzziest acts of the 2010s return with One Trip, which bathes their classic sound in a warmer light – until the buzzsaw synths and scattershot percussion explode Devotees still speak in hushed awe about the intense, hypnotic performances by Factory Floor, one of the buzziest electronic groups of the 2010s. Even the band agree: Nik Colk Void (vocalist and modular synth wrangler) wistfully remembered them as “full of carnage” during their lengthy hiatus. So what on earth went down at Mutek Montreal in 2024? Their one-off reunion show proved so transformative that it inspired Factory Floor’s first album in 10 years. Sounding uncharacteristically relaxed, opening single Continuation is a woozier take on their often grinding approach to repetition, building into blissful contentment rather than rabid euphoria. “It’s gonna be fun,” Void exhales. “It’s gonna be … easy.” This third album takes in Factory Floor’s favoured influences – brain-spinning industrial noise, eccentric acid techno, a Kraftwerkian clarity of purpose – and bathes them in a warmer light. But that’s not to say they’ve softened. Standout track Buzz Saw has the album’s toughest synth line, serrated and stomping, for what should be a new live classic. Continue reading...

articles.content: The former pontiff’s edited journals show piety and humility, but his deeper motivations remain a mystery When the cardinals in Rome elected the Argentinian Jorge Mario Bergoglio as the 266th pope of the Roman Catholic church in March 2013 – the first Latin American, the first pontiff born outside Europe since the 8th century, the first Jesuit and the first to take the name Francis (after Saint Francis of Assisi) – many of us lapsed Catholics gave a small cheer. Here was a man who looked fair to change the increasingly fusty and conservative, authoritarian and admonitory, tendencies of his two predecessors. Bergoglio seemingly did not want the ceremonial trappings of the office – he’d bought himself a return ticket home to Buenos Aires and caught the bus back to the Vatican guest house where the other cardinals were staying, insisting he would not be moving into the papal apartments overlooking St Peter’s Square. Continue reading...

articles.author: Jude Rogers
articles.content: (Last Night from Glasgow) Russo’s latest album Pe Unde Trece Dorul, roughly translated as Where Longing Goes, is full of surprises – and shows what a fantastically versatile singer she is Long based in Scotland, Lizabett Russo returns to her native Romania for her fifth album of idiosyncratic, spectral folk. Having defied her parents’ wishes to leave the country age 18 and commence her musical journey, she travelled through Transylvania’s remote villages to learn doine (songs) and strigături (traditional rhymed shouts/calls), and named her album after a song taught to her by farmer Maria Dulău, a woman awarded a title to aim for by the Romanian National Institute of Heritage: Living Human Treasure. “Dorul” is like the Welsh hiraeth or Galician saudade , referencing longing and homesickness, and “trece” explains how these feelings travel, wander and pass. Released by the label that also put out Dick Gaughan ’s startling R/Evolution box set, Russo’s album begins like an update of Fourth World music created by trumpeter Jon Hassell and Brian Eno. A sly two-note guitar riff, Tim Lane’s soft drums, and Călin Han’s slowly blown kaval flutter coolness into the air, then Russo joins, multi-tracked and layered in harmony. Her voice is fantastically versatile: gentle yet agile on Bujori (Peonies), sprightly and knowing on Frumoasă-i Nevasta Ta Măi Ghită (Your Wife Is Beautiful, Ghită), It’s also chillingly eerie on Cine Aude Gura Mea (Whoever Hears My Mouth), an a cappella that glistens in shivering reverb. Continue reading...

articles.content: They weathered excess, illness and being dropped and defrauded, but Echobelly are happily back as a duo. Ahead of a new album, they recall the weird fans and cliquey bands of the 90s In 1994, Oasis toured the US for the first time, and a legend quickly emerged: these were Britain’s latest rock’n’roll renegades, who went berserk on crystal meth before a Los Angeles gig and almost split up afterwards. But Sonya Madan remembers it differently. Her band Echobelly were also touring the US that year, and the two groups hung out backstage at each other’s gigs. “I’m gonna blow a myth!” she hoots. “For me, half the stuff about Oasis was made up by their press people. The people around them were partying; everyone was, including us, but it wasn’t that much. Liam was such a sweetheart, I used to go drinking with Noel, we were all mates.” Continue reading...

articles.author: Simon Jenkins
articles.content: The last shake-up, in the 1960s, was based on pure anti-technological snobbery. Let’s put vocational learning back in the heart of our cities What is it about the EU student fees debate that means it has almost derailed Andy Burnham’s Brexit reset? Can the issue be that important? The answer is simple – and, I am sure, personal. Before Brexit, the EU’s citizens, among them its diplomats, were paying the same as UK citizens to have their children’s English perfected at a UK university. Now, some pay up to three times that figure . To put it mildly, they have an interest in persuading the UK government to slash fees. As of now, the issue is still deadlocked. The total cost of meeting the EU’s demand and reducing EU student fees to the new British rate of £9,790 a year has been put at an astronomical £570m a year for Russell group universities alone. Burnham has declined to answer the question of who would foot the bill. Indeed, it is difficult to understand why British taxpayers should subsidise the education of wealthy Europeans. But the cost would then fall on individual universities. The University of St Andrews estimates it would lose a devastating £12m annually. Simon Jenkins is a Guardian columnist Continue reading...

articles.content: Figures indicate England’s players have far more rugby miles in their legs than Saturday’s opponents but Borthwick has managed to balance heavy schedule The prevailing narrative emerging before England’s rematch with New Zealand on Saturday is that the All Blacks are running on fumes. The forwards coach, Jason Ryan, has said that “there is not much juice in the tank” while Graham Henry, who led them to the 2011 World Cup title, has continued the theme in even starker terms. “It’s the end of the season and we’re buggered. They’ve just got no gas in the tank.” It is understood that narrative has raised a number of eyebrows within the England camp. The view, as England seek to clinch a third straight win over New Zealand for the first time in the history of the fixture, is best summed up as, “welcome to our world”. We are nearing the end of a gruelling year for the All Blacks, who give the impression they cannot wait for their season to end, but the grind in England, that which led to Maro Itoje being ordered to take the summer off, is at the very least comparable. Continue reading...

articles.author: Kathryn Hughes
articles.content: A lexicographer reveals the surprising origins of common zoological turns of phrase, from fat cats to fur babies Anyone who has grown up in the country knows that cows come home. They do it at tea time, like clockwork, because an unmilked cow is an uncomfortable cow. So how did “till the cows come home” come to mean never? Stranger still, when the phrase first appears in a 1587 commentary on St Paul’s epistle to the Galatians, there is only one cow. By the time playwrights Beaumont and Fletcher take it up a few decades later, their characters are kissing and drinking till the cow – still single – comes home. What began as a promise of endless pleasure has become a sigh of futility. Jeremy Butterfield’s Metaphor Zoo is full of such linguistic metamorphoses. Butterfield is a lexicographer by trade, the man the OUP entrusted with revising Fowler’s Modern English Usage. His guiding text is Lakoff and Johnson’s Metaphors We Live By (1980), which argues that metaphors don’t just colour how we speak but structure our thinking. In this sprightly but well-grounded book (metaphor alert), Butterfield asks what mental patterns lie behind the hundreds of animal phrases in English. Then in Johnsonian fashion, he sets about tracing the original, dating each through the Oxford English Dictionary and watching as it goes walkabout. Continue reading...
articles.description: A lexicographer reveals the surprising origins of common zoological turns of phrase, from fat cats to fur babies Anyone who has grown up in the country knows that cows come home. They do it at tea time, like clockwork, because an unmilked cow is an uncomfortable cow. So how did “till the cows come home” come to mean never? Stranger still, when the phrase first appears in a 1587 commentary on St Paul’s epistle to the Galatians, there is only one cow. By the time playwrights Beaumont and Fletcher take it up a few decades later, their characters are kissing and drinking till the cow – still single – comes home. What began as a promise of endless pleasure has become a sigh of futility. Jeremy Butterfield’s Metaphor Zoo is full of such linguistic metamorphoses. Butterfield is a lexicographer by trade, the man the OUP entrusted with revising Fowler’s Modern English Usage. His guiding text is Lakoff and Johnson’s Metaphors We Live By (1980), which argues that metaphors don’t just colour how we speak but structure our thinking. In this sprightly but well-grounded book (metaphor alert), Butterfield asks what mental patterns lie behind the hundreds of animal phrases in English. Then in Johnsonian fashion, he sets about tracing the original, dating each through the Oxford English Dictionary and watching as it goes walkabout. Continue reading...
articles.title: The Metaphor Zoo by Jeremy Butterfield review – how animals influence our language

articles.author: Andy Beckett
articles.content: ‘Andy time’ may frustrate the media and voters impatient for change – but after years of short premierships and rushed policies, isn’t this the reset Westminster needs? Andy Burnham is making a lot of people impatient. Political journalists, pro-EU activists, climate campaigners, fossil-fuel lobbyists, recipients of welfare benefits, advocates of welfare cuts, enemies of neoliberalism, enthusiasts for renationalisation, members of the armed forces and even cabinet colleagues: all are waiting for the prime minister to make big decisions, and thus reveal the true nature of his administration, four months after its beginning. Since his Manchester mayoralty, some of Burnham’s co-workers have had a phrase for his tendency to take things at his own tempo: “Andy time”. He lets interesting conversations overrun, likes to ponder issues without being rushed, and pushes back crucial announcements. The unveiling of his 10-year plan – a typically ambitious but loose Burnham timespan, and one of his government’s pivotal moments – has been repeatedly delayed. According to the website Politico, it has been pencilled in for 17 December, the final day of the parliamentary calendar. Andy Beckett is a Guardian columnist Continue reading...

articles.author: Amy-Jane Beer
articles.content: Berwickshire: Between the grey and the red formations, a staggering 65 million years passed. And the Scottish man who figured this out put science into a spin “Who wants to see some reeeally important rocks?” The question sorts my holiday companions into two distinct types, and the self-selecting nerds set out on a blustery clifftop walk. To the north-east, the 320m-year-old volcanic doorstop of Bass Rock contrasts with the edgy artifice of Torness nuclear power station, gleaming in low sun like a radioactive Lego brick. We’re going in search of an even more consequential contrast, but one that is a little harder to see. A series of interpretation stations on the path to Siccar Point encourages us to notice two distinct rock types, old red sandstone and greywacke , and to understand that each was formed in different ways at different times. The greywacke originated in a Silurian ocean 435m years ago, the sandstone in hot deserts of the late Devonian period, 370m years ago. It’s also important to understand that, given enough time, rock can be lifted, rotated, folded and weathered away. That’s what happened to the greywacke, long before the sandstone was laid down on top. Continue reading...

articles.author: Eoghan Gilmartin
articles.content: Santiago Abascal’s party has adopted radical ideas from France and beyond. If it joins a PP coalition, it would be a morale boost for allies across the continent It was a scene few would have imagined possible in Spanish politics until recently. Flanked on stage by Catalan flags, the far-right Vox leader, Santiago Abascal, addressed a packed campaign rally in Girona, where he promised “to defend Catalan identity” against supposed “Islamisation”. He urged his audience to confront what he claimed was “the primary challenge” of a new “caliphate” across Spain. For a fringe party that made its breakthrough in 2018 by demonising Catalonia’s independence movement, it was a striking change of emphasis, reflecting a strategic shift that has brought Vox to the brink of power. When the results of this Sunday’s snap general election become clear, there is a strong likelihood that centre-left PM Pedro Sánchez will be forced out, with Vox as kingmakers and junior coalition partners to the traditionally dominant rightwing People’s party (PP). The perpetually dour Abascal may lack the charisma of Trump or Italy’s Giorgia Meloni, but Vox is projected to increase its vote share from 12.4% in 2023 to close to 20% . It has achieved this surge not by moderating its rhetoric as it draws closer to power, but by embracing some of the most radical positions on immigration from across the European far right. A place in government for the party could, in turn, embolden its allies across Europe, as France, Italy and Poland prepare to go to the polls next year. Continue reading...

articles.author: Xan Brooks
articles.content: The acclaimed director has announced his latest film Tender Loving Care will be his last. He talks about coming to terms with a life-changing condition and how he would have loved to have made a big budget modern-day movie Mike Leigh and his partner, the actor Marion Bailey, were knocking around at home last Christmas, looking for a good film to watch and constantly coming up short. Finally, Leigh had a brilliant idea. Why not put on Topsy-Turvy, his 1999 costume romp about the making of The Mikado? Problem solved, perfect choice. “It’s not like a habit,” he says hurriedly. “I don’t sit there watching my films every night like Gloria Swanson in Sunset Boulevard. It’s just that Topsy-Turvy happens to be a very enjoyable watch.” The way Leigh sees it, his films are like children. They’ve outgrown him, moved on, but it’s nice to check the family ties are still strong. Some are sunny (Life is Sweet; Happy-Go-Lucky) and some are dour (Naked; Hard Truths), but they all share the same DNA, the same real-world interests and tragicomic mindset. He can’t choose between them; he’ll defend each one to the death. Then he pauses and says, “But I’ve got a soft spot for Meantime.” Continue reading...

articles.author: Lucy Mangan
articles.content: The comedian knows how to make perfectly relaxing TV – even as he tries heart-racing new experiences with celebrity pals. From flying a plane loop-the-loop with Mel Giedroyc to bungee jumping with Joanne McNally, it is bliss Alan Carr’s Great Big Bucket List, in which burgeoning national treasure since last year’s win on The Celebrity Traitors Alan tries out an array of experiences accompanied by celebrity pals, is filler TV of the most obvious kind. But this particular varietal has a twist. In this show in which the presenter tries out an array of experiences accompanied by celebrity pals, the presenter feels under no pressure to complete any of the tasks he doesn’t fancy. This makes the Great Big Bucket List the programme of my dreams and Alan my soulmate, my spirit animal, my safe space. Who wants to see people suffering? Pushed beyond their comfort zones? Not me. Why is the world so obsessed with making people uncomfortable? Comfort is the aim . Comfort is great . Comfort is everything . Continue reading...

articles.author: Brian Logan
articles.content: Soho theatre, London The standup throws himself into ‘13 or 14 pieces of humour’ that confirm his gifts for escalating everyday apercus into absurd delights Paul Foot made quite the impression with 2023’s Dissolve , a mid-career breakout from his oddball groove. The Future confirms the 52-year-old as a comic any audience could enjoy, and – to some degree – develops his newfound interest in the real world and the circumstances of his own life. Not that it begins with any seriousness of purpose, as our host throws himself into a series of escalating set pieces built on everyday apercus – how reassuring we find it, say, when a Chinese restaurant is frequented by Chinese diners. Then comes the swerve, which is less well integrated, and less remarkable, than in the show’s predecessor, but affecting nonetheless. Before that, the first half is all about Foot’s free-standing bits (“about 13 or 14 pieces of humour”, he calls them): concentrated bursts of observational comedy, in which he inflates a workaday premise to absurdity and beyond. The etiquette of British funerals; over-excitement at food served on sizzling hot-plates – Foot constructing teetering towers of nonsense from it all with a voice and range of facial expression evoking British comedy at its ooh-missus, nudge-nudge heyday. Continue reading...

articles.content: Almost 10,000 women and girls who took part in nationwide protests in October give testimony about disrupted menstrual cycles For three years, Naïma Di Piero says she barely had a period. The 46-year-old charity worker, who suffers from endometriosis, takes the contraceptive pill to suppress her menstrual cycle. But two days after being exposed to police teargas during France’s nationwide protests on 17 October, she began bleeding heavily. French police fired about 22,000 teargas grenades at protesters on 17 October at the height of the protests – equivalent to two grenades every three seconds (over 10 hours of maintaining order). Continue reading...

articles.content: Liam Delap can exploit Chelsea’s defensive woes while Senne Lammens is under pressure against Brentford Nottingham Forest’s last couple of seasons have been a story of good runs and bad runs, but it may help to know that last season’s encounters with Chelsea both presaged changes of fortune. After they lost to Chelsea in October, a seventh defeat in 10 winless games, Forest’s form improved and they won seven of their next 12 in all competitions. But after beating Chelsea in May, their seventh victory in a 10-game unbeaten run, Forest’s form dipped dramatically and they have won only twice since. Oliver Glasner’s criticism of players whose “standards [are] not high enough” is clearly designed to raise them. Time will tell if it has worked but the key man this week is one who should have no issues with motivation and whose English is at least decent. Liam Delap, facing the side that signed and swiftly discarded him, could really trouble Wesley Fofana and Levi Colwill. The Chelsea centre-back pairing were described as playing like “two novices” by Jamie Carragher after they were outfought by Dominic Calvert-Lewin last week. “Until they sign that dominant centre-back and leader, they’ve got absolutely no chance of achieving anything,” Carragher concluded. Simon Burnton Continue reading...

articles.author: Ed Aarons at Selhurst Park
articles.content: Football seasons can pivot on certain moments and Thomas Frank will hope that Crystal Palace’s turning point came 17 minutes from full time here. Deservedly trailing to Mamadou Sarr’s goal having been second best throughout against Real Sociedad, this game – and perhaps the south London club’s entire trajectory – was turned on its head after Jon Martín was sent off for denying Jean-Philippe Mateta an equaliser. The France striker made no mistake with his penalty before Dwight McNeil – who made up for scoring an own goal in Saturday’s defeat by Coventry capped an extraordinary comeback in Frank’s first home match since succeeding Pierre Sage. Despite Yéremy Pino’s saved penalty in stoppage time and a number of other chances that were squandered, Dean Henderson pulled off a stunning late save to seal the victory and revive Palace’s Europa League campaign. Suddenly Palace have hope where there appeared to be none and the Premier League’s bottom side will head into Sunday’s crucial showdown with Hull with a spring in their step. Continue reading...

articles.author: Jack Seale
articles.content: Ella Purnell is back as a meek but murderous journalist who bumps off bad men. But this isn’t a powerful feminist-revenge tale and it certainly isn’t funny – thankfully, the story is just about saved when a copycat killer arrives Rhiannon Lewis (Ella Purnell) has a nosebleed. It keeps embarrassing her at work and interrupting her when she’s trying to go against her timid nature and assert herself in the office: in nervous or stressful times, pop goes her right nostril. If that weren’t enough of a distraction, at home she has her boyfriend’s corpse stashed in the freezer, concealed beneath an unusual quantity of petits pois. We’re back for a second season of Sweetpea, the crimson-flecked comedy drama where the macabre meets the mundane. In 2024’s first season, local newspaper receptionist Rhiannon was a downtrodden wallflower, if that’s possible, who never got over a childhood during which her mother abandoned the family and her schooldays were ruined by bullying. Having been driven to psychopathy by a thousand microaggressions perpetrated by heedless, selfish men, she found her groove by murdering two boorish strangers before kidnapping her old school bully Julia (Nicôle Lecky) with the intent of killing her. When she discovered Julia’s boyfriend was abusive, Rhiannon offed him instead and allied with Julia. Between them they deflected the attentions of inquisitive junior detective Marina (Leah Harvey), who correctly guessed the identity of the serial killer but was, like her nemesis Rhiannon, a young woman to whom nobody ever listens. Continue reading...
